# Results — Study 387 (Economic-Surprise-Index)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Citi's **Economic Surprise
Index** — the desk gauge of "is the data beating expectations?" — tested on a **transparent,
public-data proxy**. CESI is proprietary and there is no free history of analyst forecasts, so
we **construct** a surprise index from six monthly FRED real-activity series: each month's
change minus its **trailing-12-month average** (a labelled stand-in for the consensus),
z-scored and averaged. We then ask whether a high index (data beating) predicts higher forward
SPY returns. Offline & deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every
number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | FRED monthly (`PAYEMS`, `INDPRO`, `RSAFS`, `UMCSENT`, `HOUST`, `DGORDER`) + yfinance SPY (public, no key) |
| Window | 1993-01-31 → 2026-05-31 (**401** month-ends; **33.3** years); as-of **2026-06-22** |
| Surprise index | per-series (Δ − trailing-12m mean), z-scored on a trailing 36m std, averaged; **PROXY** for Citi CESI |
| ESI stats | mean **−0.08**, std **1.19**, fraction of months > 0 ≈ **48%** |
| Entry / costs | 1-month execution lag; timing backtest charges 10 bps one-way per turn; SPY price-only |

> **Proxy caveat (named on the Signal axis).** Our consensus is a **trailing average**, not
> the Street's published forecast — so the surprise is mechanically an *autocorrelation* signal
> on macro momentum, and runs high coming out of recessions (data beats a depressed average)
> exactly when equities stage their largest recovery rallies. The verdict does **not** hinge on
> the proxy's exact weights: it hinges on the fact that the conditional excess over the base
> rate is small and statistically insignificant, and that a monthly ESpos>0 timing rule
> *underperforms* buy-and-hold once it sits out of an up-drifting market.

## The signal — forward SPY returns after a 'beat' month (ESI > 0) vs the base rate

1-month entry lag; the unconditional column is *all* overlapping forward windows over the same
tape (the honest base rate). Welch *t* compares the conditional mean to the unconditional
mean; the placebo *p* is the share of 20,000 random same-size date draws whose mean forward
return **beats** the beat-month set.

| horizon | n beat-months | cond. mean | cond. win-rate | base mean | base win-rate | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-month  | 191 | **+0.92%** | 64% | +0.96% | 65% | **−0.10** | 0.549 |
| 3-month  | 190 | **+2.87%** | 72% | +2.83% | 72% | **+0.06** | 0.473 |
| 6-month  | 187 | **+6.60%** | 80% | +5.79% | 76% | **+0.89** | 0.148 |
| 12-month | 184 | **+13.38%** | **88%** | +12.01% | 82% | **+1.00** | 0.134 |

Read it carefully. The "ride the surprise" story would want a *large, significant* excess. What
we get is a **small, horizon-dependent** bump: essentially **zero excess at 1–3 months** (the
horizon the announcement actually moves), and a positive-but-insignificant ~1.4-point excess at
12 months (Welch **t = 1.00**, placebo **p = 0.13** — a random 184-date draw matches it ~1 time
in 7). At 1 month the conditional mean is *below* the base rate. The macro information is
already in the price; the monthly-sampled surprise adds nothing the null can't explain.

## Tradability — the timing rule *loses* to buy-and-hold (the decisive number)

Hold SPY when the ESI (known one month earlier) is positive; otherwise go to cash (long/flat)
or short (long/short). 10 bps one-way per turn; SPY **price-only** (no cash yield credited —
which *flatters* the timing rule, since it ignores the interest it would earn while flat).

| rule | exposure | turns | net ann. return | net ann. vol | **net Sharpe** | buy-&-hold Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **long / flat** | 48% | 215 | +6.3% | 9.5% | **0.66** | **0.78** |
| **long / short** | 100% | 429 | +1.0% | 15.1% | **0.07** | **0.78** |

Even crediting the timing rule with **zero** opportunity cost while it sits in cash, the
long/flat ESI rule earns a **lower Sharpe (0.66) than simply holding (0.78)** — you give up
return by being out of the market ~half the time in a tape that mostly rises, and the surprise
signal doesn't recoup it. The long/short version is a near-flat **0.07**: betting *against*
stocks on 'miss' months is a direct fight with the equity risk premium. There is no version of
this that beats buy-and-hold. **MIRAGE.**

## Robustness — the result is flat in the threshold

| 'beat' threshold | n events | cond. 12m mean | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| −0.5 (loose) | 337 | +11.7% | **−0.23** | 0.620 |
| **0.0** (sign) | 184 | +13.4% | **+1.00** | 0.134 |
| +0.5 (strict) | 54 | +13.7% | **+0.78** | 0.234 |

Loosening to −0.5 turns the excess *negative*; tightening to +0.5 thins the sample and weakens
the *t*. There is no threshold at which the 12-month signal clears t = 2.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, and a flat signal stays flat

On a deterministic monthly series with an AR(1) surprise index and a SPY-like price, with a
**planted** forward edge (next month's return loaded on the current surprise):

| planted edge | n beat-months | cond. 6m mean | base 6m mean | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no edge) | 208 | +4.77% | +4.38% | **0.47** | 0.267 |
| **0.04** (large edge) | 208 | +12.40% | +8.48% | **2.22** | **0.003** |

With **no** planted edge the test stays well below t = 2 (it cannot manufacture significance
from a noise signal). A genuine planted edge drives t to **2.22** and the placebo p to **0.003**
— the inference detects a real edge when one exists. The control proves the machinery is
unbiased, so the real-tape *t* of ~1.0 is what an *absent or tiny* edge looks like, not a
broken detector.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The folklore is partly real: forward returns after a 'beat' month are
  positive, and the 12-month win-rate (**88%**) is high. But the *excess* over the
  unconditional base rate is small (~1.4pp at 12m), **fails the t ≥ 2 bar** (t = 1.00, placebo
  p = 0.13), is ~zero at the 1–3-month horizons the data actually moves, and *inverts* at a
  loose threshold. Literature support + a positive-but-insignificant point estimate ⇒ **WEAK**,
  not REAL. (Survivorship-free; the named confound is the *trailing-average consensus*, which
  makes the surprise an autocorrelation signal aligned with post-recession recovery drift.)
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The ESI>0 timing rule earns a **lower Sharpe than buy-and-hold**
  (0.66 vs 0.78 long/flat; 0.07 long/short) — and that is *before* crediting the cash yield it
  ignores while flat. Being out of an up-drifting market on 'miss' months costs more than the
  surprise signal returns. There is no NAV-scale edge.
- **"Free nowcast"? — BUSTED.** "Buy when the data beats" sounds like a free macro edge, but a
  surprise measured against a trailing average is mostly the market's own recovery drift in a
  costume — priced fast, sampled monthly, and indistinguishable from luck at t = 1.0.
